newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean stocks end lower on yen, business worries.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean stocks end lower on yen, business worries.

text.p: A renewed weakening of the Japanese yen against the dollar combined with political and financial concerns to push South Korean stocks down on Monday, traders and brokers said.
The Korea composite price index closed down 6.88 points or 1.01 percent to 672.10.

Analysts said the Seoul bourse would take its cue for the remainder of the week from the yen/dollar rate and the response of Korean financial markets to continuing troubles -- real and rumoured -- in corporate Korea.

"To some extent the fate of the Korean market will be determined by things happening outside Korea, meaning the yen, and to what's happening politically and financially within the country," said Henry Morris, managing director of Coryo International (H.K.) Ltd, a securities firm.
Export-related share prices in Seoul rose early on Monday on news that the yen had leapt as high as 117.60 to the dollar in early Monday trading in Tokyo, analysts said.
The yen began to slide in late morning trading and by mid-afternoon it appeared that it was too early to declare a yen rally had begun. It was trading at 119.22/55 late in Tokyo.
Seoul stocks that would benefit from a stronger yen rose sharply. A strong yen would make Korean goods from computer chips to cars more competitive in global markets.

Shares of Hyundai Electronics Industries Co Ltd soared 1,700 won to 39,000. Its shares were also helped by the company's announcement it had developed the world's "fastest" one gigabit synchronous dynamic random access memory chip.
Samsung Electronics Co Ltd shares closed up 1,100 won to 61,000, while the third leading chipmaker, LG Semicon Co saw its share price climb 700 won to 28,200.
Shipbuilding shares also rode the morning's yen strength.

Two of the top three shipbuilders, Daewoo Heavy Industries and Samsung Heavy Industries, went limit-up, rising 400 and 670 won to 5,400 and 9,120, respectively. The third, Hanjin Heavy Industries rose 630 won to 8,680.
But traders said the yen's brief climb against the dollar was the only good news on the Seoul bourse.
"Other than that all the news on the market is bad news," said S.W. Choi, chief trader with Schroders Securities. "There is a bunch of bad news."
Shares of Midopa Department Store fell by their daily limit to 10,200 won. Those of Dainong Corp, flagship of Midopa's parent Dainong Group, also fell limit low to 3,500 won.
Midopa was rumoured to be having liquidity problems. The company denied the rumours.
"The sentiment now is that after the giant defaults we've had, no one is willing to support a company in trouble," said Casey Choe, trader at Union Bank in Switzerland.

Traders said the widening scandal surrounding presidential son Kim Hyun-chul also dampened investor sentiment. A Kim associate reportedly has told prosecutors that a construction company deposited more than one billion won in a bank account suspected of being opened on Kim's behalf.
"All this news is very negative for the market," said Jinki Chung, of Kyobo Securities sales department.
